title: Adaptive Output Composability and SDK Bindings — PRD (WIP)
body:
Executive summary:

This PRD proposes an approach for a composable streaming output model and SDK binding patterns that make tool-calling and structured output ergonomics easier for developers while preserving low-latency partial responses and robust resume semantics. Instead of a single monolithic streaming frame format, we introduce layered transforms (prefix framing, typed action frames, composable filters) which clients can opt into. The goal is to unblock multi-step tool flows, localizable transform logic, and incremental validation without adding server-side complexity to every request.

Problem statement:
- Current streaming contracts are either freeform text or deeply opinionated typed frames; both create friction: freeform streams are hard to reliably parse into actions, and rigid typed protocols force server-side decisions that break backwards compatibility.
- SDK ergonomics for tool-calling are brittle: clients often need to implement heavy reconciliation, token-level stitching, or replicate server logic to reconstruct partial tool inputs.
- Resuming interrupted sessions with partially-completed structured payloads (e.g., nested tool calls) is error-prone.

Goals (what success looks like):
- Provide a minimal core streaming frame set that supports: progressive text tokens, structured frames (JSON/CBOR), and action signals (call, start, commit, rollback).
- Make SDKs provide optional "binding layers" that handle: lazy tool resolution, client-side reconciliation, and safe rehydration of partial structured outputs.
- Ensure incremental adoption: hosted API continues to support current simple streams; composable transforms are opt-in per-request via flags.
- Observable rollouts: telemetry metrics for frame decoding failures, rehydrate success rate, and average extra RTT due to binding overhead.

Non-goals:
- Not aiming to design a complete distributed transactions system for multi-tool sagas.
- Not replacing existing typed-output PRDs that target heavy contract guarantees (we target pragmatic ergonomics).

Personas and primary user journeys:
- Frontend engineer (mobile/web) building chat UI that displays partial text while rendering suggested actions. Wants minimal client code to handle action buttons that map to tool calls.
- Platform engineer integrating Redwood Hosted into workflow orchestration. Wants deterministic replay after interrupted runs and low bandwidth overhead.
- SDK maintainer who needs a pattern that supports both small clients (JS) and large services (Go, Java) with similar semantics.

Proposed API surface (high level):
- request flags: "composable_output": boolean, "binding_profile": string (optional), "resume_token": string (optional).
- streaming frames (sequence of JSON-ish envelopes over existing stream):
  - TEXT_DELTA: {type: "text", delta: "..."}  // lowest overhead
  - STRUCT_FRAME: {type: "frame", format: "json", id: "f1", payload: { ... }}  // arbitrary structured blobs
  - ACTION_SIGNAL: {type: "action", opname: "lookup_price", phase: "start|ok|err|commit|rollback", ref: "a1", meta: {...}}
  - TRANSFORM_HINT: {type: "xform", name: "truncate-html", params: {...}}  // hints for client transforms
  - CHECKPOINT: {type: "checkpoint", token: "tkn-...", cursor: 12345}  // safe resume points

Key design notes:
- Frames are orthogonal: clients can ignore STRUCT_FRAME and just render TEXT_DELTA. Servers can emit both in parallel (text for low-latency UX, frames for deterministic parsing).
- ACTION_SIGNAL phases are intended to let clients render intermediate UI (e.g., spinner, failed call) without waiting for a full structured commit.
- CHECKPOINT tokens are short-lived but cover enough state to rehydrate partial frames and outstanding actions.

SDK ergonomics: binding layers and lazy resolution patterns:
- SDKs will expose a small core API for streaming consumption and an optional "binding" helper that accepts a binding profile. Binding profiles encode how to map action names to platform tool adapters and how to resolve incomplete frames.
- Lazy binding: SDK records action signals and defers actual tool invocation mapping until application code registers a handler or until a commit-phase arrives. This reduces churn when UIs open but user never triggers action.
- Rehydration helper: given a CHECKPOINT token, SDK will fetch minimal resume state (server endpoint) and replay frames into a virtual event stream that client handlers can process as if continuous.

Example client flow (textual pseudo):
1) Client starts streaming with composable_output=true.
2) Server emits: TEXT_DELTA -> STRUCT_FRAME(id=f1, payload={"recommendations": [...]}) -> ACTION_SIGNAL(ref=a1, phase=start) -> TEXT_DELTA
3) Client binding layer sees ACTION_SIGNAL(start) -> registers ephemeral UI button. If user presses, SDK maps ref a1 -> handler that sends tool invocation to either server-side tool or registered local adapter.
4) When tool completes, server emits ACTION_SIGNAL(ref=a1, phase=commit, meta={result_ref: "f2"}) and STRUCT_FRAME(f2, payload={...}).

Migration and backward compatibility:
- If composable_output flag absent, server emits existing stream frames.
- New SDKs default to passive mode (parse frames but do not enforce). Binding only occurs if application opts in.

Telemetry and observability:
- Metrics to produce: frame_decode_errors, average_frames_per_session, percent_sessions_using_bindings, resume_success_rate, avg_latency_addition_due_to_bindings.
- Tracing: attach trace ids to CHECKPOINT tokens so resume paths are linkable to original request traces.

Security and privacy considerations:
- STRUCT_FRAME payloads may contain PII; default retention rules apply (short retention for resume tokens).
- Binding profiles must be explicit about allowed adapter endpoints; SDKs must require explicit registration of remote tool adapters to avoid accidental exfiltration.

Rollout strategy:
- Phase 0: internal dogfood in Solutions Engineering with server emitting parallel TEXT_DELTA + frames. SDKs in passive parse-only mode.
- Phase 1: external beta for 20% of orgs; enable binding helpers in JS and Go SDKs. Collect telemetry and refine frame shapes.
- Phase 2: GA with docs, migration guides, and optional server-side validation for frames when binding_profile present.

Open questions and trade-offs:
- How large should CHECKPOINT tokens be? Tradeoff between resume fidelity and token size. Suggest include only references to server-side snapshot ID.
- Binary frame formats (CBOR) vs JSON text frames: binary is smaller but harder to inspect in logs. Favor JSON for initial rollout.
- Should we expose a formal schema registry for STRUCT_FRAME payloads? Could help typed clients but increases coupling. For now, keep schema optional and encourage documented binding profiles.

Next steps:
- Align with serving-runtime on emitting parallel frames without new load (action signals are lightweight).
- Prototype binding helper in JS SDK (focus on lazy binding and rehydrate flow).
- Integrate checkpoint tokens into existing tracing path and design rotation/TTL.
- Draft developer guide with examples for common patterns (action buttons in chat, offline replay for orchestration).

Notes to reviewers / todo checklist:
- Reviewers: product-hosted-api, eng-serving-runtime, sdk-js.
- TODO: finalize frame JSON envelope names and error codes (owner: Liam).

References and previous work: existing streaming and typed-output sketches in product-hosted-api plus client SDK experiments in GH PRs (see linked_artifacts).

Appendix: sample minimal binding_profile (pseudo):
{
  "name": "chat-ui-v1",
  "actions": {
    "lookup_price": {"adapter": "server:/tools/price", "safety": "require-consent"},
    "open_url": {"adapter": "client:open-url", "allowed_origins": ["app.example.com"]}
  },
  "validation": {"allow_untyped_frames": true}
}
